summary: Describes how a network operator can ask for DNS servers to be delegated for the reverse lookup zone of a 6to4 IPv6 address block. The request uses an ordinary DNS delegation interface, and the requester is authenticated mainly by its source address and checked against the 6to4 prefix it owns. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A phone book can list names for numbers, and also numbers for names. This paper explains how to sign up for the number-to-name side for a special kind of address.

questions: how does 6to4 reverse dns authenticate clients
subtitle: How a 6to4 site asks for DNS servers to be delegated for its own reverse lookup zone, with its source address as the proof.

tldr.problem: Reverse DNS lookups need a delegation path from the DNS root to the zone holding the PTR records, but 6to4 sites get IPv6 addresses from their IPv4 address, so their upstream provider may not support IPv6 at all and will not set up that delegation.
tldr.mechanism: A single zone, 2.0.0.2.ip6.arpa, is delegated only at the 48th bit, one delegation per site. A web service reached over TLS lets a client on a 6to4 address enter its name servers, after checking that they respond and agree, and it can only manage the /48 that matches its own source address.
tldr.outcome: The RFC picks plain, explicit delegation over schemes that alter DNS server behavior. It admits that address-based authentication is weak and that a reverse mapping should not be trusted. RFC 8996 later updated it.

today: RFC 5158 is an Informational RFC, and it was updated by RFC 8996. The text says 6to4 is intended as a transition mechanism for a limited period, and IANA has delegated the 2.0.0.2.ip6.arpa domain.

sections.title: Why 6to4 Needs Reverse Delegation
sections.content:
6to4 (RFC 3056) lets isolated IPv6 sites talk over the public IPv4 Internet. A 6to4 router combines its IPv4 address with a dedicated IPv6 prefix to make a site prefix, and local hosts build their addresses from it. A site can reach IPv6 without getting IPv6 service from its upstream provider.

A reverse lookup turns an address back into a name. It needs a delegation path from the DNS root down to the servers for the zone that holds the PTR records for that address. For ordinary IPv6 addresses the path follows address block delegation. For 6to4 addresses it would have to follow IPv4 delegation, and a site whose ISP has no IPv6 support cannot be expected to have such records.

The RFC lists four wanted properties: deployable with minimal overhead or tool development, no impact on existing DNS software and operations, efficient name lookup, and no damage to DNS security functions.
sections.eli5: Imagine a street where houses get their numbers from a different system than the post office uses. The post office has no idea how to write the house numbers in its book, so the houses need a way to sign up themselves.

sections.title: The Approaches Considered
sections.content:
The RFC summarizes four ways to make reverse lookups work and then rejects three of them.

  • Conventional delegation. The trouble is piecemeal deployment: an upstream provider may offer no IPv6 and so have no 6to4 reverse delegation, and IPv4 sub-delegations are not consistently recorded. Operators would have to "hop over" the provider's block.
  • Guessing a non-delegated server. An altered server would look up the matching in-addr.arpa servers. An isolated 6to4 site uses a single IPv4 /32 address, so it is improbable that it has an explicit in-addr.arpa delegation.
  • Local servers at reserved addresses. The query is decoded and rewritten to a constant value. This needs sites to reserve addresses and generates spurious traffic.
  • Synthesized responses. A pseudo host name is made up from the address. That turns one invalid DNS object into another.

The conclusion is to support conventional standard delegation and to cut the administrative cost by giving each 6to4 site a way to manage its own delegation.
sections.eli5: There were four ideas for fixing the missing phone book entries. Three of them involved guessing or making things up, so the authors chose the plain one: write the real entry in the book, and let each owner do it.

sections.title: How a 6to4 Site Gets Its Prefix
sections.content:
A 6to4 network is an isolated IPv6 network: IPv6 hosts plus a dual-stack router connected to the local IPv6 network and the outside IPv4 network. The IPv4 address used to build the prefix is that of the router's external IPv4 interface.

The RFC's example: if that interface has the address 192.0.2.1, local IPv6 clients share the common prefix 2002:{192.0.2.1}::/48, which is 2002:C000:201::/48 in hex. All hosts share that /48 whatever local IPv4 addresses they use in dual-stack mode.

This is why delegation is done per site: one site corresponds to one /48 prefix and one IPv4 /32 address.
sections.eli5: The router's outside address is turned into a neighborhood code, and every computer inside the network starts its address with that same code.

sections.title: The Delegation Service
sections.content:
The specification uses a single delegation level in the 2.0.0.2.ip6.arpa zone (the ip6.arpa zone is from RFC 3596), delegating only at the 48th bit. Delegation zone files are run with a low TTL, in hours rather than days or weeks, and updated with dynamic DNS updates (RFC 2136).

The service is a web server reached over TLS (RFC 4346) with an https: URL, so that proxy caching cannot disrupt the source-address-driven selection and the service cannot be readily mimicked. It runs on a dual-stack IPv4/IPv6 server. A client with a 6to4 source address gets a conventional DNS delegation interface for its own /48 and nothing else. Anyone else gets a description of the process.

Before a delegation is entered, the manager checks the target servers over IPv4 and IPv6 to make sure they respond, are consistent, and are authoritative for the zone. These conditions should hold:

  • At least one primary and one secondary server are configured.
  • Both are online, reachable, correctly configured and mutually consistent, meaning the same SOA RR and identical NS RRSets.
  • The request comes from the 6to4 source address of the requesting client.

The server should throttle delegation requests made to any single IP address, and redelegation requests for any single 6to4 zone, so it is not a denial of service platform. Each active delegation has an email contact, taken from the SOA RNAME or entered in the interface, which is told of changes. Every delegation is checked every 30 days. On failure the contact is told and a second check is scheduled 14 days later. If that fails too, the delegation is removed automatically.
sections.eli5: A website looks at where you are coming from. If you come from a 6to4 network, it lets you fill in the form for your own network and nobody else's, and it phones the servers you name to check they really work.

sections.title: Trade-offs and Known Issues
sections.content:
The RFC credits the design with fully automated, on-demand operation where a site can only manage itself. It also lists weaknesses.

  • Clients inside a 6to4 site could change the delegation without the site administrator knowing. The local administrator can add access controls such as a firewall configuration.
  • A site with a dynamically assigned external IPv4 address can inherit stale reverse entries from earlier users. The RFC recommends a static IPv4 address, or updating the delegation at each address assignment.
  • The flat zone file may grow considerably. The RFC estimates the upper bound on the order of millions of entries, and notes that 6to4 is meant as a transition mechanism, and that the value of reverse delegation is questionable.
  • An enterprise using 6to4 internally would need an internal private zone for reverse lookups.

An IPv4 address controller, for example a provider that also offers IPv6, may want to block use of the scheme. The operator should allow such blocking upon application.
sections.eli5: Doing it yourself is easy, but anyone on your network could also do it, and the list could get very long. The paper says so honestly.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
The system gives only rudimentary assurance that a request can change only the matching 6to4 reverse domain. Address-based authentication is not robust because addresses can be spoofed. The RFC therefore warns that reverse delegation does not reliably validate a domain name or an IP address, and that no conclusions should be drawn from whether a reverse mapping exists.

A client can name any server as a DNS server, which could direct the checking system to query any host. The throttling of requests per IP address and per 6to4 zone mitigates that. For a general threat analysis of 6to4, including address spoofing in 2002::/16, the RFC points to RFC 3964.

IANA delegated the 2.0.0.2.ip6.arpa domain according to instructions from the Internet Architecture Board.
sections.eli5: The website trusts where you say you are coming from, and that can be faked. So nobody should believe a reverse entry just because it exists.
